questions.prompt: A sinusoidal voltage is applied across an ideal capacitor. A student finds the average power over one cycle. Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: The factor \(\tfrac12 V_p I_p\) is the average power only when voltage and current are in phase. A \(90^\circ\) shift makes the average of the product zero: the capacitor stores energy for a quarter cycle and returns it over the next. Frequency changes the current, not that average. An ideal inductor does the same.
steps: In sinusoidal steady state the capacitor current leads the voltage by \(90^\circ\).
That product oscillates at twice the drive frequency and has average zero.
The average power is \(\tfrac{1}{2} V_p I_p\), the same product used for a resistor.
reasons: The quarter-cycle shift makes the average of \(v i\) zero. The in-phase formula does not apply.

questions.prompt: A resistor \(R\) is driven by \(v(t)=V_p\cos(\omega t)\), with \(V_p\) the peak voltage. Write the average power using the name \(Vp\) for \(V_p\) and the name \(R\) for the resistance.
questions.explanation: The average of \(\cos^2\) over a cycle is \(1/2\), so \(P=V_p^2/(2R)\). Using \(V_p^2/R\) forgets that average and treats the peak as if it were a DC voltage. Using \(V_p^2/(4R)\) replaces the peak by an RMS value and then halves a second time. The frequency does not appear.
questions.figure_alt: Instantaneous power that stays non-negative and ripples twice per cycle.

questions.prompt: The US 'wall-socket' voltage has a peak value of about 170 V. What is its RMS value?
questions.explanation: For a sinusoid, \(V_{\mathrm{rms}}=V_{p}/\sqrt{2}=170/1.4142=120.2\ \mathrm{V}\) (the familiar \(120\ \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}}\)). Common mistake: dividing by 2 (85 V) or multiplying by \(\sqrt{2}\).

questions.prompt: A load has voltage amplitude 10 V (peak) and current amplitude 2 A (peak), with the current lagging the voltage by 60°. What is the average power, \(P=\tfrac{1}{2}|V||I|\cos(\phi_{v}-\phi_{i})\)?
questions.explanation:
\(P=\tfrac{1}{2}(10)(2)\cos(60^{\circ})=10\times 0.5=5\ \mathrm{W}\). The \(\cos(60^{\circ})=0.5\) is the power factor.
Common mistake: forgetting the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) for peak values (10 W) or ignoring the phase (10 W).

questions.prompt: A 50 Ω resistor has the voltage \(v(t)=20\cos(\omega t)\ \mathrm{V}\) across it. What is the average power it dissipates?
A load has impedance \(Z=6+j8\ \Omega\) and the peak current through it is 5 A. What is the average power, \(P=\tfrac{1}{2}|I|^{2}\cdot\mathrm{Re}\{Z\}\)?
questions.explanation:
Only the resistive part dissipates: \(P=\tfrac{1}{2}|I|^{2}\cdot\mathrm{Re}\{Z\}=\tfrac{1}{2}(25)(6)=75\ \mathrm{W}\).
• 125 W uses \(|Z|=10\ \Omega\) instead of Re{Z} (it would be the apparent power \(\tfrac{1}{2}|I|^{2}|Z|\)).
• 150 W omits the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) (as if I were an RMS value).
• 100 W uses the reactance 8 Ω, which stores energy rather than dissipating it.

questions.prompt: Each element below is in sinusoidal steady state. Select every one that absorbs a positive average power.
options: A resistor with a sinusoidal voltage across it.
A series combination of a resistor and an inductor, with a nonzero resistance, carrying a sinusoidal current.
questions.explanation: Average power is \(\tfrac12 \mathrm{Re}(V I^\ast)\) with peak phasors. A resistor has voltage and current in phase, so the real part is positive. An ideal capacitor or inductor has them a quarter cycle apart, so the average is zero. A series inductor does not remove the resistor's average power.

questions.prompt: A voltage is \(v(t)=3+4\cos(\omega t)\) volts (a 3 V DC offset plus a 4 V peak sinusoid). What is its RMS value?
questions.explanation:
Mean square: ⟨v²⟩ \(=\) ⟨9 \(+24\cos(\omega t)+\) 16cos²(ωt)⟩ \(=9+0+16/2=17\). The cross term averages to zero, and \(\cos^{2}\) averages to \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).
\(RMS=\sqrt{17}=4.123\ \mathrm{V}\).
In other words, the DC and AC parts add in mean-square power: \(V_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}=V_{\mathrm{DC}}^{2}+V_{p}^{2}/2\). Common mistakes: \(3+4/\sqrt{2}=5.83\ \mathrm{V}\) (adding RMS values) or \(7/\sqrt{2}=4.95\ \mathrm{V}\) (treating the peak value 7 V as if the whole waveform were sinusoidal).
questions.figure_alt: Waveform of a 4 V peak cosine riding on a 3 V DC level.

questions.prompt: A load \(Z=30+j40\ \Omega\) is driven by \(v(t)=100\cos(\omega t)\ \mathrm{V}\). What is the average power absorbed by the load?
questions.explanation:
I \(=V/Z=100/(30+j40)=100/(50\angle 53.13^{\circ})=2\angle-53.13^{\circ}\) A.
\(P=\tfrac{1}{2}|V||I|\cos(\phi_{v}-\phi_{i})=\tfrac{1}{2}(100)(2)\cos(53.13^{\circ})=100\times 0.6=60\ \mathrm{W}\). (Check: \(\tfrac{1}{2}|I|^{2}\mathrm{Re}\{Z\}=\tfrac{1}{2}(4)(30)=60\ \mathrm{W}\checkmark\).)
The product \(\tfrac{1}{2}|V||I|=100\) is the 'apparent power' (volt-amperes); the power factor 0.6 cuts it to the real power. Common mistake: answering 100 W (ignoring the phase between v and i).

questions.prompt: Preview of slew rate. A later skill says a sinusoid \(A\cdot\sin(\omega t)\) has a maximum slope of \(A\omega\), so an amplifier with slew rate SR can only produce an undistorted peak amplitude A up to the frequency \(f=SR/(2\pi A)\). An op-amp is rated to deliver 12.5 mW of average sinusoidal power into a 1 kΩ load, and its slew rate is 2 V/µs. At what frequency (in kHz) can it still deliver that full power without slew limiting?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: find the peak amplitude from the power: \(P=V_{p}^{2}/(2R)\) ⇒ \(V_{p}=\sqrt{2PR}=\sqrt{2\times 0.0125\times 1000}=5\ \mathrm{V}\).
Step 2: \(f=SR/(2\pi V_{p})=(2\times 10^{6}\ V/s)/(2\pi\times 5\ \mathrm{V})=63.66\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
Common mistake: using \(V_{\mathrm{rms}}\ (3.54\ \mathrm{V})\) as the amplitude in the slope formula, which would give 90 kHz.

questions.prompt: Preview of reading datasheets. An op-amp datasheet says the output can swing \(\pm 10\ \mathrm{V}\) (peak) into a 2 kΩ load. What is the maximum average power a sinusoidal output can deliver to that load, in mW?
questions.explanation:
For a sinusoid, \(P=V_{p}^{2}/(2R)=100/(2\times 2000)=25\ \mathrm{mW}\) (equivalently \(V_{\mathrm{rms}}=7.07\ \mathrm{V}\), \(P=50/2000=25\ \mathrm{mW}\)).
Datasheet figures for swing are peak values, so be careful to use the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\). Common mistake: \(V_{p}^{2}/R=50\ \mathrm{mW}\).

questions.prompt: Preview of bias points. A common-source amplifier has a DC (bias) supply of \(V_{\mathrm{DD}}=3\ \mathrm{V}\) and bias current \(I_{D}=1\ \mathrm{mA}\). The signal at the drain across \(R_{D}=2\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) is a sinusoid with 0.5 V peak amplitude. What percentage of the DC supply power appears as average AC signal power in \(R_{D}\)?
questions.explanation:
DC supply power: \(P_{\mathrm{DC}}=V_{\mathrm{DD}}\cdot I_{D}=3\ \mathrm{V}\times 1\ \mathrm{mA}=3\ \mathrm{mW}\).
AC signal power in \(R_{D}\): \(P_{\mathrm{AC}}=V_{p}^{2}/(2R_{D})=0.25/(2\times 2000)=62.5\ \mu\mathrm{W}\).
Ratio \(=62.5\ \mu\mathrm{W}/3\ \mathrm{mW}=2.083\%\). This is why bias (large-signal) power and signal (small-signal) power are analyzed separately.
Common mistake: forgetting the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\ (125\ \mu\mathrm{W}\to 4.17\%)\).
